response.sql:
WITH lab_data AS (
    SELECT 
        p.SEX,
        (CAST(l.CPK AS REAL) / l.GPT) as ratio
    FROM Patient p
    JOIN Laboratory l ON p.ID = l.ID
    WHERE p.SEX IS NOT NULL AND p.SEX != ''
    AND l.CPK IS NOT NULL AND l.GPT IS NOT NULL AND l.GPT != 0
),
group_avgs AS (
    SELECT 
        SEX,
        AVG(ratio) as avg_ratio
    FROM lab_data
    GROUP BY SEX
),
first_mean AS (
    SELECT AVG(avg_ratio) as mean_value FROM group_avgs
),
above_first AS (
    SELECT g.SEX, g.avg_ratio
    FROM group_avgs g, first_mean f
    WHERE g.avg_ratio > f.mean_value
),
second_mean AS (
    SELECT AVG(avg_ratio) as mean_value FROM above_first
),
above_second AS (
    SELECT a.SEX, a.avg_ratio
    FROM above_first a, second_mean s
    WHERE a.avg_ratio > s.mean_value
)
SELECT 
    AVG(a.avg_ratio) as ratio_average,
    AVG(a.avg_ratio - f.mean_value) as avg_exceed_first,
    AVG(a.avg_ratio - s.mean_value) as avg_exceed_second
FROM above_second a, first_mean f, second_mean s

assumptions.assumption: "Above" is interpreted as strictly greater than (>) rather than greater-than-or-equal-to (>=). The phrase "keep the groups whose average is above it" uses > for both filtering stages.
Division by zero (GPT = 0) is treated as a missing ratio and filtered out. If CPK = 0 with non-zero GPT, the ratio 0 is valid and retained.

alternatives.interpretation: "Above" means greater-than-or-equal-to (>=) in both filtering stages, allowing groups with average equal to the mean to be retained.
